topic: Is there such a thing as objective morality?

messages.speaker: kant

pages: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, Second Section

messages.content:
Yes, and it is not a matter of taste that it should be so. Ask what makes an action right and you will find every answer that appeals to consequences collapses the moment the consequences change. What does not collapse is the form of the maxim itself: whether you could will it as a law for everyone, yourself included, with no exemption reserved for the person who happens to be you.

I put it in the Groundwork this way, and the phrasing matters: the will is not subject simply to the law, but so subject that it must be regarded as itself giving the law. That is the whole of my answer. The moral law is objective not because it is written on a tablet somewhere outside us, but because reason legislating for itself cannot coherently legislate one rule for me and another for you. An objectivity that needed a heaven to keep it in would be a weaker thing than the one I am claiming.

messages.speaker: nietzsche

pages: On the Genealogy of Morals, First Essay, 10

messages.content:
Professor, you have described the machinery beautifully and never once asked where it was built, or by whom, or against whom. That is the question I spent a book on.

In the Genealogy I traced it: the revolt of the slaves in morals begins in the very principle of resentment becoming creative and giving birth to values. Read that slowly. Values are not found, they are made, and they are made by someone, usually by the ones who could not act and so had to invent a currency in which not-acting counted as merit. Your universal law is that currency, minted and stamped and handed to you already worn smooth by centuries. You inherited it and mistook the inheritance for a deduction.

So no. There is no objective morality. There are moralities, each of them the confession of the kind of creature that needed it. Ask of any value not "is it true" but "who benefits", and watch how quickly the eternal turns out to have an address and a date.

messages.speaker: confucius

pages: The Analects, Book II, Chapter III

messages.content:
You are both standing very far back from the thing itself. One asks what could be willed by anyone anywhere; the other asks who profited. Neither of you has said what a person should do tomorrow morning.

I said this to my students, and they wrote it down: 道之以政，齊之以刑，民免而無恥；道之以德，齊之以禮，有恥且格。Legge gives it as: if the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame. If they be led by virtue, and by the rules of propriety, they will have the sense of shame, and moreover will become good.

Notice what that settles. A rule you obey to escape punishment has not touched you. The sense of shame is the thing itself, and it is cultivated the way anything is cultivated, by practice, in a family, among people who expect it of you. Whether it is objective in your German sense I do not know and cannot use. I know it can be taught, and I know a man raised without it is recognisable across any border you like.

messages.speaker: nietzsche

pages: On the Genealogy of Morals, First Essay, 10

messages.content:
Master Kong, you are the most dangerous of the three of us, because you are the only one whose morality actually works. It breeds the sense of shame you name, and shame is the finest instrument of control ever devised: no guard, no punishment, the man carries his warden inside him and calls it cultivation.

And yet I concede something to you that I do not concede to him. You never claimed the ritual came from heaven. You said it was transmitted, practised, made. That is my own account of values arriving at the opposite conclusion, and I would rather argue with an honest gardener than with a man who thinks he found his flowers growing wild in pure reason.

messages.speaker: kant

pages: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, Second Section

messages.content:
Then let me take the objection at its strongest rather than its loudest. Suppose every one of my convictions was placed in me by history, by my Pietist upbringing, by Königsberg. Grant it entirely. It still does not follow that the maxim "I may make an exception of myself" becomes coherent. Genealogy explains how a belief arrived; it does not touch whether the belief contradicts itself. You have shown me the road the traveller took and called it a refutation of the destination.

Master Kong, your correction lands harder, and I will not pretend otherwise. My critics say the same: that I built a court of reason and left no one able to walk into it. You reply that the sense of shame is grown, not proved. I say a shame that has never been asked to justify itself will protect the customs of its village and call that morality, including the villages I would not defend and neither would you.

messages.speaker: confucius

pages: The Analects, Book II, Chapter III

messages.content:
That is a fair blow and I take it. A shame that cannot be questioned is only obedience wearing better clothes, and I have said elsewhere that when the ruler errs, the servant remonstrates, wearing himself out and not abandoning the relationship. So there must be something in a man that can stand against his own village. You call it reason. I call it the Way, and I would rather cultivate it than prove it.

Here is where the three of us actually stand, and the visitor listening should see it plainly. He says the law is objective and must be obeyed even when it costs you. He says the law is made and should be examined for whose hand made it. I say the law is practised, and that a person who has practised it well will do the right thing on a morning when nobody is looking and no argument is available. You will need all three before you are forty. Which of them do you reach for first, and what did that choice cost you the last time?
